title: Microbial Activation of Terrestrial Phytogenic Silica Cycling
content:
Abstract

Phytogenic silica (pSi) is a bio-reactive phase of the terrestrial silicon (Si) cycle; however, the mechanisms governing its fate and mobility remain elusive. Plants sequester Si to form pSi, which is inherently embedded within the organic matrix of their biomass, resulting in organic matter-associated pSi (OpSi). Following biomass decomposition, OpSi and pSi are released into soil pools where they may transition into colloidal phases that serve as pivotal drivers for the transport and biogeochemical transformation of associated elements. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized microbial-driven engine governing OpSi and pSi mobility. We hypothesized that bacteria release OpSi and pSi by enzymatically consuming the organic matrix and degrading the particle coatings. This process triggers a shift in interfacial reactivity that markedly increases the surface charge and colloidal mobility of pSi via electrostatic repulsion. To test this hypothesis, we utilized a model OpSi and pSi colloid pair prepared from rice straw and Bacillus velezensis to quantify evolving biophysical interactions. Micro-morphological and surface charge analyses confirmed the presence of an intact organic sheath shielding the pSi core. This organic shield maintains a low surface charge density on OpSi (i.e., 5.7 ± 0.5 site nm−2) and negligible bacterial repulsion, effectively keeping pSi stagnant. When the organic sheath is consumed by microbes, the exposure of the high-charge silica core causes the surface charge density to escalate dramatically, reaching 34.1 ± 0.7 site nm−2 upon the complete conversion of OpSi to pSi. This microbially driven “activation” transforms stagnant pSi into a highly mobile phase, thereby increasing its mobility in the environment.
